comment: The Learning Center curriculum — a graduated path for NON-TECHNICAL people to direct an AI agent to build real software, safely. Ecosystem-first (not file-first); the agent appears in Unit 1; runtime/sandbox before toolkits; honest about ships-today vs north-star. Rebuilt 2026-06-13 from audit+consultation workflows.

units.title: Why Workbooks
units.dek: The shift underneath all of this — and who it changes things for.

lessons.title: Why Workbooks
lessons.teaches: The problem/solution case for the ecosystem across people, teams, and organizations — and why this is the durable, future-proof shape, framed indirectly around the shift to directing software rather than hand-building it.

units.title: Build by talking to your agent
units.dek: Why you can build real software now — and how to do it by describing what you want to an agent that does the building.

lessons.title: Why you can build software now
lessons.teaches: The job-to-be-done framing: you don't want 'a workbook', you want software shipped. Workbooks is an ecosystem where you describe outcomes in plain English and an agent builds them in a safe sandbox. This is the activation 'why' that replaces the file-format opener.

lessons.title: Telling your agent what you want
lessons.teaches: Level 1->2 of the maturity ladder: describe the outcome, not the implementation; give complete, consistent context; specificity is the single biggest factor in output quality. Includes 3 editable starter-prompt cards (madlibs: 'Build me a [tool] that [does X] from [my data]').

lessons.title: The loop: prompt, look, redirect
lessons.teaches: Level 2: iteration is a loop, not one perfect prompt. Prompt -> evaluate -> refine -> redirect. When to add context vs. start over. Delegation is not abdication — you stay the reviewer and keep the publish button.

lessons.title: Reading what your agent did
lessons.teaches: Level 2->3: review AI work like an untrusted colleague — the sniff-check, spotting drift and failure modes, and the unfakeable ledger as your trustable record. A builder-facing, de-jargoned version of did-it-do-well grounded in the real wb toolkit eval surface.

lessons.title: Your first workbook, start to finish
lessons.teaches: The single worked narrative every analog front-loads and we have zero of: a marketer ships a small tool — prompt -> agent builds -> you review -> ship — told as one continuous story threading the L1->2->3 ladder. The felt first win.

units.title: The whole thing
units.dek: Now that you've built something, here's what you were standing on — the ecosystem, and the one file you walk away holding.

lessons.title: The file you end up holding
lessons.teaches: Reframed from 'Foundations = the file' to 'the core unit of an ecosystem.' Fixes the three false claims (no-server, history-in-file, one-HTML->bundle): the portable unit is a bundle that stands on a runtime; the file is the thing you hold, not the whole system.
lessons.promise: A whole working tool — its screen, its data, its history — as one file you can hold and hand to anyone, standing on an engine you own.

lessons.title: The file that remembers how it was made
lessons.teaches: How one artifact carries its own source, identity, and change history so it explains itself and proves where it came from. Soften machine-wipe portability and per-author attribution to match git.ex reality.

lessons.title: The plain language underneath everything
lessons.teaches: Everything in a workbook is written in one human-readable format you could read over someone's shoulder. Soften the unrun 'models already know org' benchmark claim. Deep syntax mechanics moved to optional/linked, not front-loaded for novices.

units.title: The engine & the sandbox
units.dek: Why it's safe to hand an agent real power — the runtime you stand on, and the sandbox that means your secrets never touch the OS.

lessons.title: Where a workbook comes alive
lessons.teaches: The runtime as the load-bearing pillar: a workbook on your laptop is a document; plugged into the engine it answers requests, runs on a schedule, serves people. Soften 'thousands = resting state'; reconcile the Nexus/Dock/seam vocabulary so they don't read as four things.

lessons.title: Why a sandbox, not a Mac mini
lessons.teaches: The isolation/threat-model story — ~40% of the thesis, currently homeless. Prompt injection, data sovereignty, espionage, why-not-micro-VMs — framed as a benefit ('the agent runs in a sandbox; your secrets never touch the OS'), the most shareable, founder-original asset. Placed BEFORE toolkits because it's the motivation for handing over power.

lessons.title: Giving software powers, safely
lessons.teaches: How a workbook gets dangerous-sounding powers (internet, secrets, sending messages) with every power handed over deliberately and revocable. Fix the lowest-rung 'no secrets' claim (minimal still grants secrets + brokered sockets per policy.ex). Frame as 'you hand over powers deliberately.'

lessons.title: Putting it on the internet
lessons.teaches: What deploying actually means and why here it's one push. Fix the public-history claim (/rcp/changes returns 401 on locked/multi-tenant deploys). Maturity-marked toward the instant-push north star.

units.title: Giving it abilities
units.dek: How your agent gets real tools to work with — now that you know the engine that runs them safely.

lessons.title: Giving a workbook real abilities
lessons.teaches: What a toolkit is: existing tools and code safely handed to a workbook so it can DO things without touching your computer. Cut the unprovable app-store boast; add the maturity hedge (toolkits = least-mature prong). Now correctly placed AFTER the engine that runs them.

lessons.title: When the writing and the program are the same thing
lessons.teaches: How a document can BE the program — the words a person reads are the instructions the machine runs — and why that makes software you can trust. Gated behind the file/language lessons.

lessons.title: The one command (reference)
lessons.teaches: Demoted to a reference card: the AGENT runs wbx, not this non-technical user. Fix the three embellishments (next-hint on only 7 verbs, in-sandbox parity bails until the Dock broker, no source split-pane).

units.title: Agents that work on their own
units.dek: Once you trust the agent for one task, here's how it works when you're not watching — and how you keep it honest.

lessons.title: What an agent really is
lessons.teaches: Strip the hype: an agent is a loop — read, act, look at what happened, go again. Understand the loop and the rest stops being magic. Note tools are host-brokered. (Moved far earlier overall; the foundational concept now anchors the agent-depth unit.)

lessons.title: Agents that keep working when you're not watching
lessons.teaches: How an agent goes from a thing you chat with to a thing that runs on its own — standing watch, taking shifts, resting, and pausing to ask you. Trim ~15% lyrical filler; orient the non-technical reader.

lessons.title: Knowing whether the agent did well
lessons.teaches: The deeper review craft: measuring a good job, catching drift, and the record you can't fake. Ground in the real wb toolkit eval surface; soften the cost/speed figure. Complements the Unit 1 builder-facing review lesson with the mechanism.

units.title: Plans that run & the system that improves itself
units.dek: Your plans become the running work — and the climax: a system that helps improve itself.

lessons.title: Plans that run themselves
lessons.teaches: Why your to-do list, calendar, and project board are one plain plan a person reads and a machine carries out. Fix the two-way kanban claim (board.ex is one-way regen) and the self-running schedule (needs a keeper). CUT the autopoet doc-link from here.

lessons.title: When a plan becomes a program
lessons.teaches: The same plan that organizes your week can become a running system with no new tools, and how it changes safely while live. Maturity-marked.

lessons.title: The system that improves itself
lessons.teaches: The honest Level-3 summit and the thesis's emotional peak, relocated here from a stray doc-link. The autopoet edits the declarative config layer (toolkits/skills/defs), never host code — Phase-1 reality, brand-canon framed: 'software built in workbooks', NOT 'sites that run themselves.'

units.title: Trust, sharing & the disk
units.dek: How something you can copy infinitely stays trustworthy, private, and useful when you hand it out.

lessons.title: Proving where it came from
lessons.teaches: If anyone can copy a file, how do you know a workbook is really from who it claims? A signature that travels with the bytes and can't be faked. Best-in-set; optionally name did:key/SHA-256 once for the deep-doc bridge.

lessons.title: Sharing without oversharing
lessons.teaches: A file you send is a file you've given away completely — so how do you share the app without handing over the private data? The public shell vs. the protected core. Trim the seal recap (overlaps proving-origin); disambiguate 'seal.'

lessons.title: Keeping a secret inside a file you hand out
lessons.teaches: Part of a file given to everyone can be readable only by the one person holding the right key — locked in the open, opened only on permission. Note the ETS key-store is non-persistent (restart = revoke).

lessons.title: A place to keep things that travels with the work
lessons.teaches: Every project needs somewhere to keep files; here it lives inside the workbook, travels when you send it, and can be queried like a spreadsheet. Reconcile the single-HTML claim (egress is a bundle: HTML + separate SQLite). Merged from the dissolved disk unit.

lessons.title: When the work outgrows one file
lessons.teaches: What happens when a project gets big — reaching outside data, remembering by meaning, swapping in real storage — without changing how it works. Soften pull-to-disk + 'memory=files'. Optional/back-half.

units.title: Under the hood
units.dek: Optional, for the curious — the why behind the magic, and the one idea everything is wearing different clothes of.

lessons.title: Why none of this is magic
lessons.teaches: A no-code tour of how the pieces fit — the tiny engine at the center, and the single idea everything is. The two redundant endings (the-browser + under-the-hood) dissolve into this ONE capstone. Scope no-I/O to lib.rs; one line that the capability boundary lives in the seam.
